extracted.intended_audience: authors preparing and submitting Papers to ACM CHI 2022 (researchers in HCI preparing conference submissions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for preparing and submitting a Papers contribution to the ACM CHI conference, describing what reviewers will assess and how authors should present work to maximize acceptance chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the submission’s contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of the submission’s contribution to the field of HCI; this provides the Program Committee with a basis for assessing the significance of the contribution, and for judging whether all the reviewers agree on what the contribution is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the contribution explicit in the abstract and the paper so reviewers can identify the novel claim being made; clear articulation helps reviewers agree on what is being evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall recommendation categories
rubrics_metrics.description: An overall recommendation of the review outcomes: Accept with minor revisions, Revise and resubmit (major revisions required), and Reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand these categories to set expectations; if recommending revisions, provide clear bullet points of required changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall rating (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: An overall rating for the paper based on the contribution it makes to the field of HCI, from 1 (Reject) to 5 (Strong Accept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This numeric rating summarizes perceived strength of the contribution and interacts with reviewer recommendations and PC decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise rating (1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rating of the reviewer’s own expertise in the topic area of the submission, from 1 (No Knowledge) to 4 (Expert); this helps members of the Program Committee to resolve conflicting views on submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should select the best matching subcommittee so reviewers with relevant expertise assess the work; expertise ratings influence how much weight is given to particular reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of the contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance of the paper’s contribution to HCI and the benefit that others can gain from the contribution: why do the contribution and benefit matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contribution and its significance are the most important criteria; papers must clearly and significantly advance HCI and explain who benefits and how. State in the abstract and discussion why the contribution matters to researchers/practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality of the work: what new ideas or approaches are introduced? We want to emphasise that an acceptable paper must make a clear contribution to Human Computer Interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how the contribution goes beyond prior publications; cite prior work (including your own), explain limitations you overcome; novelty in methods or data collection can earn credit but is not a substitute for a clear contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity of the work presented: how confidently can researchers and practitioners use the results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide appropriate arguments, analyses, evaluations, or data tailored to the contribution type; explain why chosen validation methods are appropriate. Anticipate common reviewer concerns (insufficient evidence, weak theoretical basis, unjustified design choices) and address them directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write clearly and concisely, avoid jargon, organize logically, provide the right level of detail, and use figures and tables to support the text. Proofread especially if not a native English speaker; avoid long complex sentences and regional colloquialisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant previous work / literature review
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant previous work: is prior work adequately reviewed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and integrate prior work into the narrative; explain how your work relates to and differs from key publications. Avoid merely long lists of references; focus on well-integrated, easy-to-find publications so reviewers can check context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required revisions (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of revisions required for acceptance if the reviewer’s overall recommendation is Accept with minor revisions or Revise and resubmit (major revisions required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers will be asked to provide clear bullet points of what revisions need to be made; authors should ensure requested changes are achievable within the (limited) revise-and-resubmit timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting an appropriate subcommittee
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers are reviewed by subcommittees that each focus on a subset of topics in HCI. As an author, you decide which subcommittee best matches the contribution of your research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the subcommittee that best matches your topic so reviewers with relevant expertise assess the paper; consult Selecting a Subcommittee guidance for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the contribution type explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: HCI opens up a broad range of possible contribution types; this contribution should be made clear in the abstract as well as the submission itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether your contribution is an interaction technique, case study, design/evaluation methodology, theory, system/tool/infrastructure, quantitative study, qualitative study, etc., and tailor the paper to expectations for that contribution type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the benefit to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain who stands to benefit from the contribution and how they would use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you write, keep in mind the kinds of people who would benefit and how the contribution addresses their problems; make it easy for readers to extract the practical or theoretical benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain not only what you did, but why
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain not only what you did, but also why you did it, so that readers (including reviewers) can be convinced that you made appropriate choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide justification for design choices, methodological decisions, and analyses. This helps reviewers assess appropriateness and enables others to build on your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit for originality in methods or conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers will often give credit for original approaches adopted in conducting the work, particularly if these contributed strongly to the work’s success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include novel data-collection strategies, novel evaluation approaches, or clever ways of overcoming weaknesses. Include a few examples of such originality without overwhelming the central contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency for technology-oriented and quantitative contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that are technology-oriented (e.g., a new technique or algorithm) and contributions that are quantitative studies (experiments with statistically analyzed results) are expected to be verifiable, reproducible and replicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enough detail for an independent researcher to evaluate correctness, validity, and reliability of software and analyses; provide algorithmic/statistical detail, pseudocode where helpful, and sufficient procedural detail to rerun experiments/analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency for qualitative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions that follow a qualitative research approach should be transparent about the various decisions made, and the procedures followed in the design of the research study and reporting of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain theoretical/conceptual basis, choice of methods at each stage, participant-selection process, data collection and analysis procedures, ethical considerations (anonymity, consent), researcher roles, and possible biases. Describe how themes were identified and whether conclusions reflect individual instances or general trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharing research materials
rubrics_metrics.description: While the paper should provide as much information as possible to enable verification, reproduction, and replication, some details may not be shareable within the paper itself. Reviewers welcome and expect such material to be available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post code, analysis scripts, datasets, protocols, and other materials to publicly available open-access repositories with persistent identifiers (e.g., OSF); state explicitly when material cannot be shared and why. Sharing non-sensitive analysis code is strongly encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations on reproducibility when resources are rare
rubrics_metrics.description: While some independent researchers may have difficulty fully replicating your work (e.g., if the work requires unique user populations or rare hardware), an independent researcher who has access to these resources should ideally be able to reproduce your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient procedural and technical detail so that someone with the same resources could reproduce results; explain constraints on replication where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should be supported with figures and tables where appropriate; these should be clear and easy to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures may use color but should remain usable when printed in black and white. Use visuals to clarify methods, results, and contributions rather than decorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and international readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must be written in a language that effectively communicates across national and cultural boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon, idioms, puns, and regional colloquialisms; non-native speakers should consider proofreading or professional editing. Reviewers try to assess work independent of language issues, but good English helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and demonstrate validity early
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating validity is one of the most challenging aspects; consider when planning the work and certainly before embarking on the submission how you will demonstrate your contribution’s validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluations/analyses during the planning stage appropriate to the contribution type (e.g., controlled experiment for incremental improvements, real-world deployment for systems, comparative evaluations for methodologies, argumentation/use of theory for theoretical contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the Revise and Resubmit process
rubrics_metrics.description: CHI 2022 Papers will include a revise and resubmit phase replacing the rebuttal; note that unlike typical journals, the time frame for the Revise and Resubmit process is limited, and will not allow authors to execute another extensive implementation and/or evaluation or perform complete rewrite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If required revisions would not be achievable within the short timeframe, the submission will be rejected. Plan and submit work at a stage where anticipated major tasks are reasonably complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘As-is’ review expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that unlike journal papers, CHI Papers are reviewed mostly on an ‘as-is’ basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the conference review cycle allows limited revision time, submissions should be as complete and polished as possible at submission time.
